name: Hedi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Langermann, Cindy. 1994. A Phonological Description of Hedi. Yaounde: Societe Internationale de Linguistique (SIL Cameroon). 68 pp. Corroborating tone descriptions: Langermann 1991 (Hide-Lamang comparison, sec. 4.2.4 'Hide is a tonal language'), Gathman 1994 (Some Notes on Tone in the Xedi Language), Bramlett 1996 (Preliminary investigation into the function of tone in Hedi).
catalog_quote: I will only give some general observations in regards to intonation. Much further study needs to be carried out to gain a better understanding of intonation and tone. I will not deal with tone except to say there are three phonetic tones which collapse into two phonemic tones, high and low tone. See E. Gathman (1994) for a fuller treatment of Hedi tone. To understand intonation, one must look at pause groups. These are groupings of phonological words which have boundaries caused by a pause. There seems to be a raising of pitch on the syllables where there is stress. Interrogative pause groups exhibit high or mid pitch at the beginning and have slight downdrift. When the pause group is final in the sentence, the pitch on the final syllable is lower. Non-final pause groups maintain throughout two tone patterns. Imperatives and emphasis also seems to exhibit higher pitch.
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Hdi (hdii1240) is not in the catalog. Both title-search hits are Ekkehard Wolff papers in Köppe print volumes (2004 WOCAL 4, pp. 43-65; 2006 Topics in Chadic Linguistics II, pp. 141-154) about segments, petrified suffixes and Chadic 'prosodies' (palatalization/labialization) in the Lamang-Hdi cluster — not word stress; no open copy exists (Köppe has no page for the 2004 volume; the 2006 volume is sold as print/paid PDF with no preview). Beyond the title list: the open Dictionaria Hdi dictionary intro (Frajzyngier et al. 2017) was downloaded and read — two tones, phrase-final H lowering, no mention of stress; the DNB scan of the table of contents of Frajzyngier & Shay 2002 A Grammar of Hdi was downloaded and scanned — ch. 2 Phonology has sections on consonants, vowels, syllable structure and tone (7.1-7.5) but none on stress; the chapter body remains paywalled (correct DOI 10.1515/9783110885798, ch. 2 =.9; the earlier DOI was for A Grammar of Mina and has been corrected). Of the SIL Cameroon papers already held by the project, only Langermann 1994 p. 50 mentions stress at all ('There seems to be a raising of pitch on the syllables where there is stress'), with no placement rule; Bramlett 1996 pp. 7-9 speculates about 'accentuation on the first syllable' blocking tonal perturbation. No source read states where word stress falls.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Hdi is described as a two-tone (H/L) language; the only remark on stress is that stressed syllables show raised pitch within pause groups. No source opened states which syllable of the word carries stress, so no placement rule can be given.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (Bramlett 1996 pp. 7, 9 separately speculates about 'accentuation on the first syllable' of certain reduplicated verb forms as a possible reason for blocked tone perturbation, explicitly as an unanalysed hypothesis, not a stress rule.)
new_statements.domain_note: Langermann's remark concerns intonation over 'pause groups' (phrase level), not word-level citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All SIL papers (Langermann 1991/1994, Gathman 1994, Bramlett 1996) describe the Hedi/Xədi (ALCAM 122) of Tourou, Mayo-Tsanaga, Far North Cameroon = Hdi [xed], hdii1240 (no Glottolog dialects). Langermann 1991 compares it with Lamang (lamn1239, Nigeria), a separate sister language whose stress Wolff 1983 describes; Lamang statements must not be transferred to Hdi.

new_statements.reading: Hdi is described by every first-hand source read (Langermann 1991, 1994; Gathman 1994; Bramlett 1996; Frajzyngier et al. 2017 Dictionaria intro; TOC of Frajzyngier & Shay 2002) as a two-tone language. The only mention of word stress anywhere is Langermann's impressionistic remark that stressed syllables carry raised pitch; no source states where stress falls, and the reference grammar's phonology chapter has no stress section. Bramlett 1996 speculates about 'accentuation on the first syllable' as a reason for tonal non-perturbation but does not posit a stress rule. Net: no usable word-stress placement statement exists in the accessible literature; Hdi should be coded as tonal with stress unreported.

tone_statements.citation: Peust, Carsten. 2017. Review of Zygmunt Frajzyngier, Paul Eguchi, Roger Prafé & Megan Schwabauer, Dictionary of Hdi. A Central Chadic Language of Cameroon (Köln: Köppe 2015). Folia Orientalia 54: 340-346.
tone_statements.quote: Most of the basic vocabulary of both languages is clearly akin, though with various differences of the segments and particularly of tone. The massive tonal discrepancies between Hdi and Lamang, two languages so closely related, puzzled Wolff (2013) and made him posit that Proto-Lamang-Hdi was still non-tonal and tone evolved independently in the two daughter languages. But I suspect that we must first reach firmer ground regarding the documentation of the tones of Hdi (and perhaps of Lamang as well) until serious comparative work on them can begin.
tone_statements.locator: p. 345 (review body; the two-tone statement 'the analysis of tones, assumed to be two in number' is on p. 344)
tone_statements.summary: 2 tones (H, L) assumed in the Frajzyngier sources, phrase-final H lowering; reviewer finds the published tone marking pervasively inconsistent.

sources.citation: Frajzyngier, Zygmunt, Paul Eguchi, Roger Prafé, Megan Schwabauer, with Erin Shay and Henry Tourneux. 2017. Hdi dictionary. Dictionaria 3. Leipzig: MPI-EVA.https://dictionaria.clld.org/contributions/hdi
sources.quote: The language has two tones, high and low. Tone plays an important role in both the lexicon and the syntax of the language. In the lexicon, tone distinguishes between lexical items whose segmental structure is identical. Tone also plays an important role in the coding of the semantic roles of arguments, in the reference and nominal system, in modality coding, and in virtually all constructions in the language. All high tones in phrase-final position are lowered.
sources.note: Silent on stress: the phonology sketch (consonants, vowels, syllable structure, tone) contains no mention of stress, accent, or prominence; the only 'stress' token in the whole intro is 'social stress' in the history section.

sources.citation: Bramlett, Lee. 1996. Preliminary investigation into the function of tone in Hedi. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon. 21 pp.
sources.quote: In the Lo Hi class the tone melody of the reduplicated element is not changed. This may be the result of accentuation on the first syllable bearing the Lo tone. Further analysis of the whole system may shed light as to why this form is tonally unperturbed. [...] In this L Lf form the downstep is unrealized, possibly as a result of accentuation of the initial syllable. [...] the first verb is contrastively accentuated syllable final so that a lexical Lo becomes a Hi and a lexical Hi becomes a Lo.
sources.locator: Sec. 3 (completive verb forms), pp. 7-9 (scanned page markers p-07 to p-09)
sources.note: Tone study (four lexical tone classes, downstep, tonal perturbation at verb junctures). 'Accentuation' is invoked speculatively as a possible reason why some initial-syllable tones resist perturbation; no statement of a word-stress rule.

sources.note: Substantive critique of the tone data: the dictionary/grammar analysis assumes two tones; Peust lists dozens of head-words whose tone marking contradicts itself across entries (p. 344), notes Frajzyngier 2002: 39 'all high tones in phrase-final position are lowered, but they do not become as low as low tone' as a possible partial cause, calls the tone documentation of Hdi unreliable and in need of new fieldwork (Gathman 1994 'the only study dedicated exclusively to this topic'), and reports Wolff 2013's claim that Proto-Lamang-Hdi was non-tonal (p. 345).
